about: This is the one place in the Mass where the servers pray for the priest's own forgiveness, and what they say to him is exactly what he is about to say over them — the same formula, only in the singular: “misereátur tui”, “peccátis tuis”, “perdúcat te”. Over them it will run “vestri”, “vestris”, “vos”. The priest's answer, “Amen”, is his assent to a prayer made for himself. The second formula, the “Indulgéntiam”, is missing here: the priest adds that one only after the servers' confession, and there he counts himself in.

s01.translation: May almighty God have mercy on you, and having forgiven your sins, bring you to life everlasting.

s02.narrative: The priest answers the prayer made for himself.

s04.narrative: The priest straightens up. The ministers now repeat the confession — in the same words, with the single change the missal states outright: where the priest said “to you, brethren” and “you, brethren”, they say “to you, father” and “you, father”.

w001.function: A subjunctive of wish: not “he had mercy” but “may he have mercy”. The servers do not absolve — they ask that God do it.

w002.function: The genitive of the pronoun “thou”, not the possessive adjective: misereor governs the genitive of the person pitied. The same form tui belongs to the paradigm of “thy” as well — hence the easy confusion with “tuis” (w008).

w004.function: Nominative: the subject, though it comes only fourth.

w006.function: The participle opens an ablative absolute — a phrase standing free of the rest of the sentence: “thy sins having been forgiven”.

w007.function: The subject of the ablative absolute with “dimíssis” (w006).

w008.function: Agrees with “peccátis” (w007). This is the possessive adjective, unlike “tui” (w002) — one family of words, two different jobs.

w009.function: A second subjunctive of wish, joined to the first: may he have mercy and may he bring.
